title: The Monkey King's Bridge
text:
In this Jataka tale the future Buddha was born as the king of a troop of eighty thousand monkeys. They lived in a great mango tree on the bank of the Ganges, whose fruit was so sweet that the monkey king had them strip every mango from the branches over the water, so none would float downstream and reveal the tree to men. One fruit was missed.

It drifted down to Benares, where King Brahmadatta tasted it and set out with his men to find the tree. They surrounded it at night, planning to shoot the monkeys at dawn. The monkey king leapt across the river, tied one end of a long cane to a tree on the far bank and the other around his own waist, and jumped back. The cane fell short. So he gripped a branch of the mango tree and stretched his own body to complete the bridge, and the whole troop ran across his back to safety.

The last to cross was a jealous monkey, the future Devadatta, who leapt down hard on his back and dealt him a mortal blow. King Brahmadatta had watched the whole night. He had the dying monkey king lowered gently, cared for him, and asked why he had done it. The monkey king said that a ruler must seek the welfare of those he rules, and he died content.
lesson: Leadership is tested when the plan falls short and someone has to close the gap personally. People follow, and even opponents respect, the person who takes the strain so others can cross.
people: The Bodhisatta as monkey king, King Brahmadatta of Benares, Devadatta
